title: Efficiency and the new economics of shipping’s decarbonisation
summary: Shipping lines are finally acknowledging that basic operational efficiency, previously a mere cost-saving afterthought, now offers financial incentives by avoiding regulatory penalties. This shift is driven by the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, which directly monetise every tonne of CO2 emitted, forcing owners to re-evaluate their carbon intensity. While avoiding compliance costs for thousands of tonnes of CO2 is a minimal step, this belated focus on incremental efficiency must not overshadow the urgent need for drastic fuel transition.
content:
Oskar Levander from Kongsberg Maritime writes for Splash today.

For almost two decades, efficiency has been routine good practice in shipping. Owners have cut fuel burn and improved hull and propeller performance. These useful measures were often treated in isolation as cost control. However, this approach no longer fits the complexity facing the sector, nor the larger question of how to pay for decarbonisation. Efficiency can help fund it.

The EU ETS brought shipping into carbon pricing in 2024. It covers all intra-EU emissions and half of emissions on voyages in and out of EU ports. FuelEU Maritime penalises fuels that miss a GHG intensity target that tightens with each compliance period.

The IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework would apply similar logic to the global fleet: a worldwide fuel-intensity standard backed by emissions pricing. Ships that beat the target could earn tradeable credits; those that fall short would pay into an IMO fund. Member states are due to vote on adoption in December 2026. If adopted, rules could take effect from 2028.

These regulations give efficiency and clean energy sources a new value. It can earn money to fund new fuels and supporting technology.

For example, under EU ETS, every tonne of CO2 a vessel does not emit is an allowance the owner does not have to buy or surrender. As free allocation to shipping is phased out, a container ship saving several thousand tonnes of CO2 a year avoids a large compliance cost before any fuel savings are considered.

Many owners have yet to catch up. Payback calculations based on fuel savings alone now understate the return. Hull optimisation, wind assistance, propulsion upgrades, heat recovery and digital energy management each deliver lower fuel costs, avoided ETS allowances, lower FuelEU compliance costs, and, for fleets with verified data, premiums from charterers and green finance providers.

A recent Kongsberg Maritime study shows the change that is possible. The Kamsarmax design combines hull and propulsion optimisation, integrated energy management and wind assistance on long open-sea routes. Modelled against a conventional Kamsarmax on a similar trade, it cuts fuel use by more than 40%, and by over half on the most wind-favourable routes. Every tonne of fuel saved on European trades is a tonne less exposed to EU ETS, and it reduces the vessel’s overall FuelEU compliance costs. Additionally, the wind assistance technologies also earn the vessel a FuelEU reward factor.

Owners who still judge efficiency on fuel cost alone are underestimating the return. A project that looked like a seven-year payback in 2021 could instead be a three-year payback in 2026, before any premium from a greener charter rate or better finance terms is realised.

While carbon prices are volatile, banking on future compliance savings can be risky. The caution is fair, but EU carbon prices have risen as free allowances are withdrawn. Even at a modest price, the saving from lower fuel burn over a vessel’s two- or three-decade working life can outweigh the risk of a weaker carbon market. Waiting for price certainty means waiting for something that will never come.

Efficiency is also fuel agnostic. Whether ships run on methanol, ammonia, bio-LNG, hydrogen derivatives or a mix, a vessel that needs less energy will be cheaper to run. With rules still being written and the future remaining uncertain, that flexibility is worth a great deal.

Decarbonisation is as much a balance-sheet problem as an engineering one. Efficiency is the most practical lever owners have. Those who combine small gains, prove them with verified data, and put the savings back into the transition can fund their way through the next decade.
